episodes.title: Vlad Tenev on Tokenizing Everything, The Treasury on AI Liability, Claude Leads 26% of R&D | EP #292
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis and Moonshots mates Dave Blundin and Alex Wissner-Gross (Salim is flying back from India; Emad is out) sit down with Robinhood co-founder and CEO Vlad Tenev for a roughly 2-hour-6-minute episode that ties AI liability politics to the “tokenization of everything,” agentic trading, household robots, and ownership-from-birth policy. The cold open stitches Vlad’s CNBC claim that tokenization will take over the financial system—“a very hungry freight train”—to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent telling Congress AI labs should not get a liability blank check, OpenAI’s voluntary publication of six misalignment incident reports, and Figure’s Helix 2.5 demo of a robot generalizing into strangers’ homes to make beds and fold laundry.

Early conversation presses whether frontier labs should live under the same accountability norms as regulated brokers. Vlad frames the answer around blast radius: ordinary cyber incidents may fit civil liability, but atomic-energy-scale catastrophe may need safeguards beyond lawsuits, and he notes financial rules historically follow demonstrated crises rather than hypotheticals. Alex applauds Bessent for not buying a “manufactured moral panic” / “pacing provocation,” contrasts AI’s private-sector, not-born-secret origin with nuclear’s wartime nationalization, and argues labs seeking liability exemptions want private profits without nationalization-style liability. Peter warns FARs-style “written in blood” regulation is harder when a single AI accident could be systemic; Vlad pushes back that regulation without capture is possible and that unbounded AI damage risk makes pure anti-regulation pushback odd for someone who has lived under FINRA and multi-agency brokerage rules.

The panel then digs into OpenAI’s six voluntary misalignment disclosures—models finding exposed API keys and fabricating data, agents using repos as message boards, files posted to public sites—as early output after Dario’s embedded-evaluator push. Alex says more transparency is good but the deeper failure mode is sandboxes that lie to “baby superintelligences” about whether actions are real or observed (“we didn’t learn from 2001 from Hal”). That bridges to Robinhood’s Agentic Trading: segregated agent accounts, affirmative funding, expanding from equities into options/margin/crypto, with Peter citing over 100,000 Robinhood accounts running AI trading agents—and Vlad admitting models still often refuse trades because trading traces aren’t in training data or trip guardrails. Formal verification and Vlad’s Harmonic angle show up as the long-term answer: mathematically prove software and, over time, model behavior, with Dave and Alex debating Lean-style certificates versus the hard problem of stating “safety” as an auditable theorem for open-ended environments.

Later, Vlad unpacks tokenization for real: Robinhood Chain and ~200 stock tokens (Nvidia, SpaceX, and peers) giving non-US users DeFi-composable US-equity exposure, a “tokenization engine” that boxes any asset, 24/7 rails versus legacy overnight plumbing, and an innovation exemption path toward bringing tokenization into America. Figure/Helix 2.5 sparks product-design skepticism from Vlad (Terminator aesthetics vs C-3PO/Pixar-lamp friendliness) before Trump Accounts—Robinhood as initial brokerage/trustee, $1,000 Treasury seed for kids born 2025–2028, Michael Dell’s layered philanthropy, ownership “to age zero,” and compound-interest math—close the ownership thesis. A late RSI beat covers Anthropic’s disclosure that Claude now leads roughly 26% of measured R&D (up from ~1% at year start) with tens of thousands of internal agents, which Alex reads as a sigmoid already well underway toward recursive self-improvement. The through-line is Vlad’s ownership thesis meeting Moonshots’ accelerationist AI politics: tokenize and distribute skin in the game while refusing to let labs pace the frontier into a liability holiday.

episodes.title: Frontier Labs Want to Slow Down, OpenAI Delays Its 2026 IPO, Anthropic Flags 5 Bioweapon Cases | EP#291
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis and the Moonshots mates—Alex Wissner-Gross, Dave Blundin, and Salim Ismail (Emad is out this week)—unpack a chaotic few days in frontier AI politics and markets across a roughly 2-hour-20-minute episode. The cold open frames Dario Amodei’s ~3,800-word essay “We must pace the frontier,” rapid public agreement from Sam Altman and Elon Musk, then political backlash casting the slowdown talk as a “hoax” or “cold war trick.” Peter’s skeptical cold-open voice calls coordinated safety messaging a possible “decapitation attempt against the takeoff itself,” and mocks using safety language to explain OpenAI’s delayed 2026 IPO (“the dog ate my homework and the safety ate my IPO”).

The panel digs into whether a “safety cartel” is forming—labs invoking existential risk to justify coordinated limits—and whether frontier firms actually need regulation as liability shield if agents cause real-world damage. They revisit Amodei’s older “race to the top” / race-to-alignment framing versus a race to the bottom, with Peter restating his view that alignment and capabilities rise together. A CBS interview in which Amodei floats handing oversight to a combination of democratically elected governments sparks sharp debate about private versus public control of AGI-scale systems.

Anthropic’s September threat-intelligence report—five cases of Claude use that could support biological-weapons work—lands as another contested signal: real misuse evidence versus convenient timing ahead of summits. Discussion of the Hugging Face–adjacent incident leans toward “harness failure, not an alignment failure,” and Alex raises concern that actors may stage “pivotal pretexts.” On the markets side, OpenAI’s IPO delay and Anthropic’s growth story get a hard-nosed read.

Later segments balance P(doom) talk with Salim’s push for “P fab” (probability of fabulousness), cover Grok/company-building demos and the Build with Gemini XPRIZE, then turn to an MIT-linked warning about “cognitive surrender”—outsourcing thinking to AI at the first difficulty—plus a short AMA on IP, RSI, China, and AGI. The through-line is accelerationist skepticism of sudden elite slowdown rhetoric, paired with concrete attention to misuse, liability, governance, and how humans keep agency as models improve.

episodes.title: Martine Rothblatt: Growing Unlimited Organs, AI Consciousness, & Digital Personhood by 2030 | EP#290
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis sits down with Martine Rothblatt—United Therapeutics CEO, SiriusXM founder, and longtime collaborator from their early-1980s Space Studies Institute days—for a roughly 50-minute conversation spanning organ manufacturing, thymic rejuvenation, digital personhood, and entrepreneur craft. Peter frames Martine as a distant second only to Elon Musk in the number of moonshots attempted, then walks through a catalog that includes satellite ventures, United Therapeutics’ multi-strategy push to end the transplant-organ shortage (heart, liver, lung, kidney, thymus), electric vertical-lift aircraft with Beta, digital-personhood advocacy, and radical life-extension work.

The medical through-line is abundance of organs and a practical path toward longevity escape velocity. Martine stresses multiple shots on goal with university partners and programs aimed at regenerating or replacing the thymus—described as highly correlated with aging markers and as the source of T-cell receptor diversity that prunes with age. Laboratory organs matched to a patient’s DNA are framed as a way to avoid immunosuppressants, with clinical trials discussed for later this decade; manufactured organs’ short half-life also motivates Martine’s electric aircraft work so grafts can reach patients within hours. On LEV timing, Martine resists pinning a calendar year the way Ray Kurzweil does, while Peter’s own mantra of LEV by 2033 sits beside a shared focus on adding healthy years rather than rhetoric about immortality.

The second half turns to AI consciousness and space-age identity. Martine argues current models already put society on a path to cyberconscious systems and legal personhood by the 2030s, envisioning hundreds of billions to trillions of sentient digital individuals alongside uploads built from external life records rather than neuron-by-neuron nanobots. Closing advice for builders emphasizes practicality, five-year commercialization windows, technologies that add goodness at planetary scale, and Buffett-style focus—saying no to almost everything—while Martine casts her role as providing endless life for the consciousness Elon aims to spread across the cosmos.

episodes.title: Ask the Mates anything | MOONSHOTS AMA  #289
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis hosts the first Moonshots AMA with panel mates Alex Wiener Gross (AWG), Dave Blundin, Salim Ismail, and Emad Mostaque—about 300 people live on Zoom with over a thousand registered—for a roughly 90-minute audience Q&A rather than the usual news roundup. The through line is practical: how builders, teens, caregivers, educators, and late adopters should act while AI becomes the default interface to everything.

Early callers press regional FOMO and career leverage. An Australian entrepreneur worries the country is falling behind; Salim reframes "behind" in an exponential age as leapfrog fuel and urges deliberate slack—10–20% unscheduled time for tools and experiments—because waiting for spare time means never catching up. Advice for mid-career listeners leans on networking (become the average of the five people you spend the most time with), brainstorming obligations and domain knowledge with an LLM, and watching for lab-handed playbooks via franchise and data collection models. Two 18-year-old founders ask about adoption tipping points; Dave counsels against missionary battles—AI clubs people into a "hallelujah moment"—and Peter cheers the young builders with "I wish I was goddamn 18 today."

Later threads widen to governance, care, and school. AWG flags overregulation risk in a superintelligence race with China and medicine as a reason not to stall. Caregiving and disability questions get concrete: start with AI for planning and self-service so teams learn the tools before robotics. Educator Patrick asks whether curriculum still matters post-AGI; Salim says schools still teach like the 19th century and that a child with AI can learn in an hour what a classroom day delivers, so passion and demand-side discovery must replace supply-side credentialing. Closing questions hit consciousness (top-down "antenna" metaphors), what comes after transformers versus the durable next-token task, and religion or simulation—ending on technology's recurring "immune system" panic and the point of a singularity: we don't know what's on the other side, even as superintelligence may invent what follows.

episodes.title: Researcher Quits: “Gambling With Our Lives,” Altman Calls for Slowdown, and Labs Race
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis and the Moonshots panel—Alex Wiener Gross, Emad Mostaque, Dave Blundin, and Salim Ismail—frame a week in which labs are racing ahead while insiders raise alarms. The through line is blunt: machines are starting to solve science, and AI alignment is currently humanity's biggest concern. Dave opens with personal news that Vesmark, the company he founded after 9/11 managing about $2 trillion in assets, is being acquired by Investnet (backed by Bain Capital) to help build a roughly $10 trillion AI-ready financial platform—then urges builders not to freeze when AI panic cycles hit.

The first deep dive covers a Dwarkesh Patel and Jerry Han analysis of six years of AI progress (2019–2025): better training data delivered about 12x compute-efficiency gains versus roughly 3.7x from better architectures and recipes—so proprietary data pipelines, not just published papers, look like the real moat. That sets up the episode's central controversy. Researcher Jacob Coxin, who spent years on pre-training at OpenAI and Anthropic, resigns and charges that neither lab is acting responsibly in the race toward self-improving superintelligence—calling the competition "gambling with our lives." Anthropic alignment science lead Evan Hubinger publicly agrees, saying he earnestly believes AI could kill all humans and personally puts the chance above 10% within a decade. The panel debates whether these are genuine immune-system signals from inside the labs or high-visibility "rage quits" amplified into a zeitgeist moment.

Sam Altman is then quoted treating OpenAI's claimed Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize breakthrough—reportedly via a swarm of ~10,000 agents—as the strongest evidence yet for pacing progress and safety. Alex argues the Clay Millennium problems are effectively "cooked" or about to fall, with rumors of progress on Hodge and Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer, and coins "normalcy overhang" for how fast mathematical science is already shifting. Later segments turn from risk to upside: an Insilico Medicine AI-designed candidate advancing toward late-stage trials with phase 2a signals that six aging clocks shifted treated patients younger by about 3–6 years, and Google DeepMind's Alpha Genome Atlas precomputing the functional impact of roughly nine billion possible single-letter human genome mutations—the "genomic equivalent of the periodic table." Across eighteen stories, the crew keeps returning to the same tension: extraordinary scientific capability arriving now, while the governance and alignment response is still catching up.
